bib.title: Interactive Fiction Games: A Colossal Adventure

read.skipped: Appendix B transcripts and learning-curve axis ticks skimmed (numeric noise); appendix A read in full

question: Can interactive fiction (text adventure) games serve as a testbed for language-based agents, and how well do current RL and heuristic agents do on a broad set of human-made games?
hypothesis: IF games combine combinatorial action spaces, language understanding and commonsense reasoning, so they make a good testbed for language agents.
contributions: Jericho, a learning environment for human-made IF games
A template-based action space argued to suit language generation
An empirical evaluation of learning agents across a large set of human-made games

method.summary: Introduces Jericho, an OpenAI-Gym-like Python interface to human-made IF games with score-based reward, save/load, templates, vocabulary and world-change detection. Evaluates a random agent, NAIL (heuristic, no training), DRRN (choice-based RL) and the new Template-DQN (TDQN) on 32 supported games.
method.task: text-adventure game playing (sequential decision making in language)

datasets.name: Jericho supported games (32 evaluated)
datasets.size: 32 games, max score 1 to 600 per game (Table 1)
datasets.split: DRRN/TDQN trained and evaluated per game; no held-out games
datasets.source: Infocom classics (Zork, HHGG) and community games (Anchorhead, Afflicted); github.com/Microsoft/jericho
datasets.preprocessing: SentencePiece 8000-vocab model trained on strings from human play sessions of IF games

models.name: DRRN
models.architecture: separate GRUs for narrative, inventory, location description and action text; Q(o,a) via ReLU+linear; softmax action sampling; prioritized replay

other.handicaps: world-change detection for valid actions, load/save

models.name: Template-DQN (TDQN)
models.architecture: extends LSTM-DQN; GRU observation encoder with three heads: Q(o,u) over templates and Q(o,p1), Q(o,p2) over vocabulary

other.aux_loss: supervised binary cross entropy toward valid templates/words, evenly mixed with TD error

models.name: NAIL
models.architecture: hand-crafted heuristics with map building and a web-based language model

models.name: RAND
models.architecture: uniform sampling from {north, south, east, west, up, down, look, inventory, take all, drop, yes}

training.objective: Q-learning (TD error); TDQN adds BCE valid-action loss
training.steps: DRRN 100,000 updates (16 parallel environments, 1.6 million environment interactions); TDQN 1 million environment steps (single environment)
training.seeds: 5 independent runs per game; no environment seeds set

other.hyperparameters: tuned on Zork1 and held fixed across games; values not given in the paper
other.episode_limit: terminated after 100 valid steps or game over/victory

inference.decoding: DRRN: softmax sampling over Q-values of valid actions; TDQN: template then words
inference.samples: RAND and NAIL: 1000 total environment steps; scores averaged over 5 runs; learned-agent score is mean return over last 100 episodes of learning

parameters.action_space_example: 200 templates, 700 words gives O(T V^2) about 98 million

metrics.name: raw game score
metrics.definition: mean return over last hundred training episodes

metrics.name: progress score
metrics.definition: agent score normalized by maximum possible game score, averaged across games

eval.protocol: 5 runs per learned agent per game; 32 games; per-game hyperparameters not tuned; handicaps reported per algorithm

availability.code: https://github.com/Microsoft/jericho; DRRN/TDQN at https://github.com/microsoft/tdqn; NAIL at https://github.com/microsoft/nail_agent
availability.data: games listed in Jericho; unsupported games at github.com/BYU-PCCL/z-machine-games

evidence.quote: DRRN was trained for 100,000 updates, using data collected from 16 environments in parallel.

results.claim: DRRN reaches the highest average progress across 32 games.
results.setup: 32 Jericho games, 5 runs, hyperparameters tuned on Zork1
results.quote: RANDOM 1.8%, NAIL 4.9%, TDQN 6.1%, and DRRN 10.7% completion

results.claim: No agent scored on five of the games.
results.quote: None of the agents were able to get any score on ﬁve of the games.

results.claim: The template action space is about three orders of magnitude smaller than 4-word vocabulary actions.
results.quote: a typical game with 200 templates and a 700 word vocabulary yields an action space of O(T V2) ≈98 million

results.claim: Zork1 template-action space is 115 million actions.
results.quote: Zork1 has 237 templates with a 697 word vocabulary, yielding an action space of 115 million

results.claim: A 4-word action from a 700-word vocabulary has 240 billion possibilities, of which perhaps 100 million parse and only about a hundred are valid.
results.quote: out of the 240 billion possible actions there may be 100 million that are grammatical and successfully parseable

limits: Agents trained and evaluated on the same single game; no test on unseen games (authors concede, Future Work).
Agents differ in handicaps (DRRN/TDQN use save/load, valid-action detection; NAIL none), so scores are not a like-for-like ranking; authors say they provide scores as benchmarks, not comparisons.
NAIL was developed on many of the evaluation games.
Hyperparameters tuned on Zork1 and not reported; no optimizer or learning rate in the paper.
TDQN assumes independence between template and word choices, producing invalid combinations like 'take north'.
Scores are mean over last 100 training episodes, not a separate test phase.
RL-era agents; no LLM agents evaluated.
